essays.stem: Describe how you would plan and set up a spreadsheet to record weld inspection results, so that data can be keyed in quickly and accurately.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would look at the paper inspection sheet and decide which details must be recorded, such as the record number, job number, joint ID, welder ID, date, process, weld size, result and inspector. Each detail becomes one column with a clear heading in the top row, and each inspection becomes one row. I would put the columns in the same order as the paper sheet, so that the clerk's eyes follow the form. I would set the right data type for each column: dates as dates, sizes as numbers with one decimal place, and IDs as text. I would add checks: a drop-down list for the result (Pass, Fail, Repair), a range check for weld sizes, and a list of valid welder IDs. I would freeze the heading row, add a count and total at the bottom to compare with the paper batch, and protect the heading and formula cells. Finally I would save it with a clear name and test it with a few sample sheets.
markingPoints: Decides the details needed from the source sheet: one column per detail, one row per record, clear headings
Puts columns in the same order as the source sheet
Sets suitable data types for dates, numbers and IDs
Adds validation checks such as drop-down lists and range checks
Adds control totals, protects key cells, saves with a clear name and tests it

essays.stem: Explain the difference between validation and verification of data, and give an example of each for keying in stock records.
essays.modelAnswer: Validation is a check made by the computer as data is entered, to make sure the data is sensible and allowed. It cannot tell whether the data is true, only whether it fits the rules. For example, a stock form may only accept electrode sizes of 2.5, 3.2 or 4.0 mm from a drop-down list, or a quantity between 0 and 500 (a range check), or a date in the right format. Verification is a check that the data entered matches the source it came from. For example, after keying a batch of delivery notes, a second person reads each record on the screen against the paper note, or the clerk compares the computer's total of all quantities with a total worked out from the notes. Data can pass validation but still be wrong, for example 3.2 mm keyed when the note said 2.5 mm, which is why both checks are needed. Together they keep the stock records accurate.
markingPoints: Validation: the computer checks that data is sensible and allowed by the rules
A correct validation example, such as a drop-down list, range check or date format
Verification: checking the entered data against the source
A correct verification example, such as a second-person check or comparing batch totals
Explains why both are needed: valid data can still be wrong

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to key in a batch of 50 handwritten delivery notes, and how you would check the work.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would sort the notes into order, for example by date, and check that each one is complete and readable. I would put any unclear notes aside and query them with the storeman or the supplier, rather than guess. I would work out a batch total of the quantities from the paper notes and count the notes. Then I would open the correct file, check that it is the latest version, and set up my workstation comfortably. I would key the notes in one at a time, using the Tab key and the number pad, and tick each note when it is entered, so that none is missed or keyed twice. I would save often. When I finished, I would compare the number of records and the computer's total with my batch totals. If they did not agree, I would find and correct the error. Finally, a second person would spot-check some records against the notes, and I would file the notes and back up the file.
markingPoints: Sorts and checks the notes, and queries unclear ones instead of guessing
Works out batch totals before keying
Opens the correct, latest file and keys each note in order, marking it as done
Saves often and compares the record count and total with the batch totals
Corrects errors, has a second-person check, files the notes and backs up

essays.stem: Explain how to find and retrieve information from a large data file using search, sort and filter. Give an example of when you would use each.
essays.modelAnswer: Search, using Find, is best for finding one record quickly when you know an exact detail. For example, to find job J-2417 in a list of 5,000 jobs, I would press Ctrl and F and type the job number. Wildcards, such as E70*, can find all the entries that start the same way. Sorting puts the whole list in order by one column, such as due date or client name. For example, I would sort the jobs by due date, oldest first, to see which are most urgent. I must select the whole table before sorting, so that each row stays together. Filtering hides the rows that do not meet a condition, without deleting them. For example, I would filter the inspection log to show only the welds with the result 'Fail', or only the jobs for one client. Filters can be combined, such as 'Fail' and welder W07. After retrieving the data, I would check that it makes sense before using it, and clear the filters afterwards.
markingPoints: Search or Find for one known record, with a correct example
Sort to put the list in order, with a correct example
Selects the whole table so that rows stay together
Filter to show only records that meet a condition, with a correct example
Checks the result makes sense and clears filters afterwards

essays.stem: Describe how to keep data secure and private in a small fabrication business, including passwords, access rights and the law.
essays.modelAnswer: Each person should have their own login, with a strong password that is not shared or written on the desk, and two-factor authentication where it is offered. Screens should be locked when the user leaves the desk, and placed so that customers cannot read them. Access rights should be set so that people can only see or change the data they need: for example, only the office manager changes pay records, and only the quality officer changes welder qualification records. Personal data about workers and clients, such as addresses, phone numbers, TRNs and pay, must only be used for the purpose it was collected for, kept accurate, and not given to callers or others without permission. Jamaica has a data protection law that protects this kind of information, so the business must follow it and its own policy. Files should be backed up, unknown USB sticks and email links avoided, and anti-virus software kept up to date. Old paper records with personal data should be shredded when they are no longer needed.
markingPoints: Own logins, strong passwords not shared, two-factor authentication where offered
Screens locked and placed so others cannot read them
Access rights limited to what each person needs
Personal data used only for its purpose and not given out; follows Jamaica's data protection law and the business policy
Backups, care with USB sticks and links, anti-virus, and safe disposal of old records

essays.stem: Explain how and why data should be backed up, and how you would check that a backup can be restored.
essays.modelAnswer: Data can be lost through a hard drive failure, a power cut, a virus, theft of a laptop, a fire, or someone deleting a file by mistake. A backup is a second copy kept somewhere else, so that the business can carry on. Important files, such as job records, quotations and inspection logs, should be backed up on a regular schedule, for example every day, by an automatic tool or by a named person. At least one copy should be kept away from the main computer, such as in cloud storage or on a drive stored off site, so that a fire or theft does not destroy both. Backups should be labelled with the date, and older copies kept for a time in case a problem is found late. To check a backup, I would restore one or two files to a test folder now and then, open them, and check that they are complete and up to date. I would record the test and report any failure at once, so that it is fixed before the backup is needed.
markingPoints: Gives reasons data can be lost
Backs up important files on a regular schedule, with someone responsible
Keeps at least one copy in a different place, such as the cloud or off site
Labels backups with dates and keeps older copies for a time
Test-restores files, checks them, records the test and reports failures

essays.stem: Describe how to name, store and control the versions of data files, so that the team always uses the right one.
essays.modelAnswer: The business should agree a naming rule and stick to it. A good name tells you what the file is, its date and its version, for example 2026-10_Inspection-Log_v3. Names such as 'new file' or 'Document1' should never be used. Files should be stored in a clear folder structure, for example by year, then by client, then by job, on a shared drive or cloud folder that is backed up. There should be one master copy of each working file. People should open and edit the master, rather than emailing copies around, because separate copies lead to lost or clashing changes. When a file is changed in an important way, the version number goes up, and a short note of what changed can be kept. Old versions are moved to an archive folder, not left beside the current one. Only named people should be able to change key files, and the team should be told where the current version is kept.
markingPoints: A clear naming rule with what the file is, a date and a version number
A logical folder structure on a shared, backed-up drive
One master copy is edited, not emailed copies
Version numbers go up for real changes, and old versions are archived
Edit rights limited, and the team told where the current file is

essays.stem: Explain how you would produce and check a report for the manager from stored data, such as a list of jobs due this week.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would find out exactly what the manager needs: which jobs, which details, in what order, and whether it should be printed or emailed. For jobs due this week, I would filter or query the job file for due dates from Monday to Friday, and show only the useful columns, such as job number, client, description, due date and status. I would sort it by due date, or by client if asked. I would add a clear title, the date it was produced and page numbers. Before sending it, I would check that the filter is right, for example by counting the jobs and comparing the count with the full list, and I would check a few records against the job cards. I would use Print Preview to make sure it fits the page and is easy to read. Then I would print it or save it as a PDF and send it, keeping a copy. If I found errors in the stored data, I would report and correct them.
markingPoints: Finds out exactly what the manager needs
Filters or queries the data and shows only the useful columns
Sorts it, and adds a title, the date and page numbers
Checks the result: counts, sample records against the source, and Print Preview
Prints or sends it as a PDF, keeps a copy, and reports any data errors

essays.stem: Describe how to set up a data-entry workstation, and how to work, so that you avoid strain and stay accurate over a long session.
essays.modelAnswer: The chair should be adjusted so that my feet are flat on the floor or on a footrest and my thighs are level, with my lower back supported. The top of the screen should be at or a little below eye level, about an arm's length away, and placed to avoid glare from windows. The keyboard and mouse should be close, so that my elbows are by my sides and my wrists are straight. The source documents should be on a holder beside the screen, at about the same height, so that I do not keep twisting my neck. I would keep the desk clear of drinks and clutter. While working, I would take short breaks, for example a few minutes every hour, look into the distance to rest my eyes, and stretch. I would use shortcuts, the Tab key and the number pad to cut down mouse work. Working at a steady pace, rather than rushing, keeps errors down, and I would check my work in batches.
markingPoints: Chair adjusted: feet supported, back supported
Screen at or just below eye level, at arm's length, without glare
Keyboard and mouse close, wrists straight; document holder beside the screen
Short regular breaks, eye rests and stretches
Steady pace, shortcuts and batch checks to stay accurate

essays.stem: You find that the stock records do not match what is on the shelves. Explain how you would find the cause, correct the records and stop it happening again.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would recount the items carefully, with a second person if possible, so that I am sure of the real figure. Then I would compare the records with the source documents (delivery notes, issue slips and job cards) for the period since the last correct count. This often shows the cause, such as a delivery keyed twice, an issue not recorded, a transposition error, stock booked to the wrong item code, or damaged stock thrown away without a record. I would report the difference to my supervisor before changing anything. The record would then be corrected with an adjustment that has a note of the reason, the date and who approved it, rather than simply typing over the old figure. To stop it happening again, I would suggest recording every issue at once, using drop-down lists for item codes, checking batch totals after keying, and doing regular spot counts. I would follow up to see whether the next count agrees.
markingPoints: Recounts carefully to confirm the real figure
Checks the records against the source documents to find the cause
Reports the difference to the supervisor before changing anything
Corrects the record with a noted, approved adjustment, not by typing over
Suggests and follows up changes to stop it happening again

practical1.title: Design a weld inspection log and key in a batch of inspection sheets
practical1.brief: As a group, set up a spreadsheet for a fabrication shop's weld inspection log, key in a batch of records, and check them. The assessor gives the group 25 made-up handwritten inspection sheets (job number, joint ID, welder ID, date, process, weld size, result and inspector), including two or three that are unclear or incomplete. Stage 1, design (about 45 minutes): agree the columns and headings, set the data types, and add checks: a drop-down list for the result (Pass, Fail, Repair), a range check for weld size, and a list of valid welder IDs. Save the file with a clear name in the folder the assessor gives. Stage 2, preparation: sort the sheets, list any that are unclear and query them with the assessor (who plays the inspector), and work out a batch total of the weld sizes and a count of the sheets. Stage 3, keying: each member keys an equal share of the sheets on the Centre's computer while the assessor watches. Stage 4, checking: members swap and verify another member's records against the sheets, compare the record count and total with the batch totals, and correct any errors. Stage 5: filter the log to show the failed welds, save the file, and make a backup copy in a second place. Photograph the screen at each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: 25 made-up handwritten inspection sheets (from the assessor)
The Centre's computers with a spreadsheet program
A folder for saving, and a second place for the backup (USB drive or practice cloud folder)
A blank batch-total sheet and a query list
photos: The column headings and data types set up
The drop-down list and range check working, including an entry being refused
The query list of unclear sheets, and the batch totals
Each member keying their share (one photo per member, screen only)
A member verifying records against the sheets, with corrections noted
The count and total on screen matching the batch totals
The filter showing only the failed welds
The saved file name, and the backup copy in the second place
checklist: Helped to design clear columns, headings and data types
Set up or tested at least one validation check
Queried unclear sheets instead of guessing
Keyed their share accurately, using Tab and the number pad, and saved often
Verified another member's records against the source sheets and corrected errors
Compared the count and total with the batch totals and explained any difference
Saved the file with a clear name and made a backup
Kept a good posture and took short breaks
safety: Adjust the chair and screen before starting, and take short breaks
Keep drinks away from the computers
Keep cables tidy and off the walkways
Use only the Centre's computers and folders; the data is made up, but treat it as private

practical2.title: Retrieve information from a job and stock file and produce a report for the manager
practical2.brief: As a group, answer a manager's questions from a stored data file and produce a short report. The assessor gives the group a file of about 200 made-up job and stock records (job number, client, parish, item, quantity, unit price in J$, due date and status) and a question sheet with at least 10 questions, for example: 'Which jobs for Campbell Hardware are due this month?', 'How many jobs are still open?', 'What is the total value of the 3.2 mm electrodes in stock?' and 'Which items have fewer than 10 in stock?'. Stage 1: share out the questions so that each member answers at least two while the assessor watches, using Find, sort, filter and simple formulas such as COUNT or SUMIF. A second member checks each answer. Stage 2: find and correct the three keying errors the assessor has hidden in the file (for example a transposed number or a duplicate record), noting each change. Stage 3: produce a one-page report for the manager with a title, the date, the answers, a list of the jobs due this week sorted by date, and a chart of open jobs by parish. Save it as a PDF with a clear file name, email it to the assessor's practice address from a practice account, and back up the working file. Photograph the screen at each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: A data file of about 200 made-up job and stock records (from the assessor)
A question sheet with at least 10 questions
The Centre's computers with spreadsheet and word processing programs
A practice email account and the assessor's practice address
A folder for saving, and a backup location
photos: The data file opened, with the headings visible
Each member's search, sort or filter for their questions (one photo per member, screen only)
A formula such as COUNT or SUMIF, and its result
Each hidden error found, before and after correction
The list of this week's jobs sorted by date
